steps: Given: Height of mercury column, hₘ = 0.76 m; density of mercury, ρₘ = 13.6 × 10³ kg m⁻³; density of water, ρw = 1000 kg m⁻³.
Required: Height of water column, hw.
At sea level, pressure due to the mercury column equals pressure due to the water column: ρₘ g hₘ = ρw g hw.
Therefore, hw = (ρₘ hₘ) / ρw.
Substitution: hw = (13.6 × 10³ kg m⁻³ × 0.76 m) / (1000 kg m⁻³).
Working: hw = 10.336 m ≈ 10.3 m.
Result: The height of the water column is 10.3 m.
Given: Force on the first piston, F₁ = 500 N; area of the first piston, A₁ = 5 cm² = 5 × 10⁻⁴ m²; area of the second piston, A₂ = 20 cm² = 2 × 10⁻³ m².
Required: Pressure transferred to the brake oil, P; force on the second piston, F₂.
Pressure, P = Force / Area.
Substitution: P = 500 N / (5 × 10⁻⁴ m²).
Working: P = 1.0 × 10⁶ N m⁻².
By Pascal’s principle, the pressure is transmitted equally throughout the brake oil. Therefore, F₂ = P A₂.
Substitution: F₂ = 1.0 × 10⁶ N m⁻² × 2 × 10⁻³ m².
Working: F₂ = 2000 N.
Result: The pressure transferred is 1.0 × 10⁶ N m⁻² and the force on the second piston is 2000 N.
Given: Density of sea water, ρ = 1030 kg m⁻³; depth, h = 10 m; acceleration due to gravity, g = 10 m s⁻².
Required: Water pressure on the diver, P.
Pressure in a liquid, P = ρgh.
Substitution: P = 1030 kg m⁻³ × 10 m s⁻² × 10 m.
Working: P = 103000 N m⁻² = 1.03 × 10⁵ N m⁻².
Result: The water pressure on the diver is 1.03 × 10⁵ N m⁻².
Given: Area of the small piston, A₁ = 10 cm²; area of the large piston, A₂ = 100 cm²; weight of the car, F₂ = 4000 N.
Required: Force on the small piston, F₁.
According to Pascal’s principle, pressure is transmitted equally through the liquid: F₁ / A₁ = F₂ / A₂.
Therefore, F₁ = (F₂ A₁) / A₂.
Substitution: F₁ = (4000 N × 10 cm²) / 100 cm².
Working: F₁ = 400 N.
Result: A force of 400 N should be exerted on the small piston.

items.figure: Draw altitude (m) on the horizontal axis and pressure (kPa) on the vertical axis. Plot the points (150, 99.5), (500, 95.7), (800, 92.4), (1140, 88.9), (1300, 87.2), and (1500, 85.3). Draw a smooth best-fit line through the points and extend it to altitude 0 m. The graph reads approximately 101 kPa at sea level.
steps: Given: Altitude and pressure readings are (150 m, 99.5 kPa), (500 m, 95.7 kPa), (800 m, 92.4 kPa), (1140 m, 88.9 kPa), (1300 m, 87.2 kPa), and (1500 m, 85.3 kPa).
Required: Air pressure at sea level, where altitude = 0 m.
Draw a graph with altitude (m) on the horizontal axis and pressure (kPa) on the vertical axis. Plot the given points, draw a best-fit line, and extend it to altitude 0 m.
From the graph, pressure at sea level ≈ 101 kPa.
Conversion: 101 kPa = 101 × 10³ Pa = 1.01 × 10⁵ Pa.
Result: The air pressure at sea level is 1.01 × 10⁵ Pa.

From 90 kPa on the vertical axis, draw across to the line and then down to the altitude axis. The graph gives an altitude of approximately 1.02 km.
steps: Given: Altitude and pressure readings are (150 m, 99.5 kPa), (500 m, 95.7 kPa), (800 m, 92.4 kPa), (1140 m, 88.9 kPa), (1300 m, 87.2 kPa), and (1500 m, 85.3 kPa).
Required: Altitude at which the air pressure is 90 kPa.
Draw a graph with altitude (m) on the horizontal axis and pressure (kPa) on the vertical axis. Plot the given points and draw a best-fit line.
From 90 kPa on the vertical axis, draw a horizontal line to the graph line, then a vertical line down to the altitude axis.
From the graph, altitude ≈ 1020 m = 1.02 km.
Result: The air pressure would be 90 kPa at a height of approximately 1.02 km.
Given: Increase in pressure, P = 10 N cm⁻²; area of the output platform, A = 50 cm².
Required: Extra load supported, F.
Pressure = Force / Area; therefore, F = PA.
Substitution: F = 10 N cm⁻² × 50 cm².
Working: F = 500 N.
Result: The output platform will support an extra load of 500 N.

Working: P = 1.0 × 10⁶ N m⁻².
